title: Read-Only Domain Controllers for Branch-Site Resilience and Risk Reduction
summary: Understand when an RODC is preferable to a writable DC, what it protects, and what operational limitations remain.
objective: Decide when to deploy an RODC in a branch location and explain how read-only directory data, password-replication policy and delegated local administration reduce exposure.
body_outline: RODCs are designed for locations where physical security or local administrative trust is insufficient for a writable domain controller.
Directory partitions are read-only on the RODC; writes are referred to writable domain controllers.
Password caching is controlled through Password Replication Policy, so branch authentication resilience must be balanced against credential exposure if the server is stolen.
RODC deployment does not remove WAN, DNS, replication, monitoring, backup or lifecycle requirements.
quick_check: What risk does an RODC reduce compared with a writable domain controller in a physically insecure branch site?

title: RODC in Plain English: A Branch Copy That Cannot Rewrite the Master
summary: An RODC gives a branch local directory services while limiting what can be changed or cached locally.
analogy: Think of an RODC as a branch-office copy of a central register: staff can read it locally, but changes must go back to the trusted head office.
plain_language_explanation: RODCs help support branch authentication and directory lookup without placing a fully writable copy of Active Directory in a location where physical or administrative security is weaker.
visual_hint: Show hub writable DCs replicating one-way directory changes to a branch RODC, with password caching governed separately.
quick_check: Can an RODC accept normal directory writes locally?

title: RODC Security Model: Password Replication Policy, Delegation and Failure Boundaries
summary: Examine the operational trade-offs behind RODC credential caching and delegated local administration.
architecture_notes: The RODC model reduces branch compromise blast radius by limiting local writes and allowing selective password caching rather than assuming every branch server is a fully trusted writable DC.
internals: Password Replication Policy controls which account credentials may be cached. Delegated local administration can permit server maintenance without granting equivalent administrative rights across the domain.
failure_modes: Overly broad password-cache allow lists, treating a branch RODC as a substitute for WAN/DNS design, or failing to monitor replication can erase much of the intended risk reduction.
trade_offs: Caching more credentials improves branch survivability during WAN loss but increases the number of credentials potentially exposed if the RODC is stolen or compromised.
enterprise_design_notes: Base caching policy on actual branch logon requirements, exclude privileged accounts, and document recovery actions for RODC compromise.

title: Read-Only AD Time Hierarchy and PDC Emulator Health Check
summary: Map domain time sources and verify that clients and domain controllers follow the intended hierarchy without changing configuration.
objective: Collect read-only evidence showing the domain time hierarchy, current source and offset before any time-service remediation is attempted.
prerequisites_detail: Domain-joined lab or controlled enterprise Windows systems with permission to run standard W32Time diagnostics.
environment: One client, one member server and at least one DC; identify the forest-root PDC emulator before the exercise.
topology: Domain members -> domain hierarchy -> forest-root PDC emulator -> approved upstream time source.
steps: Identify the forest-root PDC emulator with `netdom query fsmo` or PowerShell.
Use `w32tm /monitor` to compare reachable domain-controller clocks and offsets.
Record systems using unexpected local, VM-host or public time sources and escalate them for configuration review rather than changing production settings during this lab.
expected_result: Domain members trace to the intended domain hierarchy and the forest-root PDC emulator has a documented reliable upstream source.
validation: Compare observations with the approved time architecture and Kerberos troubleshooting baseline.
rollback: Not required; all actions are read-only.
cleanup: Remove any notes containing production hostnames according to local handling policy.

title: Forced DC Removal: When Metadata Cleanup Becomes Mandatory
summary: Use a controlled decision path after an unrecoverable domain-controller demotion failure or forced removal.
symptoms: A domain controller was forcibly demoted or permanently lost
Replication topology still references the retired DC
FSMO, DNS or Sites and Services metadata still points to the failed server
diagnostic_order: Confirm the DC is permanently offline and that normal demotion or recovery is no longer viable.
Inventory FSMO, Global Catalog, DNS and replication responsibilities formerly held by the server.
Follow the Microsoft metadata-cleanup procedure from a healthy replication partner.
Validate removal from Domain Controllers OU, Sites and Services, replication topology and DNS before reusing the same server name or address.
escalation_boundary: Metadata cleanup is destructive directory administration. Do not remove a reachable or potentially recoverable DC merely because it is temporarily unavailable.

title: Windows Server 2025 AD Functional Levels and Global Catalog Planning
summary: Understand functional-level interoperability, Windows Server 2025 prerequisites and the Global Catalog's role in forest-wide search and authentication dependencies.
objective: Plan functional-level changes without breaking DC interoperability and explain why Global Catalog availability must be included in DC placement and lifecycle planning.
body_outline: Functional levels determine AD DS feature availability and which Windows Server versions may run as domain controllers; they do not control member-server or workstation OS versions.
Windows Server 2025 introduces a Windows Server 2025 forest/domain functional level; all DCs must meet the target requirement before raising the level.
A Global Catalog stores a partial replica of objects across the forest to support forest-wide discovery and other directory functions.
Before raising functional levels or retiring DCs, verify replication health, backups, FSMO holders and Global Catalog placement.
quick_check: Why is installing one Windows Server 2025 DC not enough reason to raise the whole domain to the Windows Server 2025 functional level?

title: Windows Time Service in AD: Why the Forest-Root PDC Emulator Matters
summary: Trace the normal Windows domain time hierarchy and connect time health to Kerberos and authentication reliability.
objective: Explain how Windows domain members choose time sources and identify the forest-root PDC emulator's role in the hierarchy.
body_outline: Domain-joined Windows systems normally synchronize through the AD domain hierarchy rather than each system independently choosing an Internet NTP source.
The PDC emulator in the forest root domain occupies the top position in the domain hierarchy unless another reliable time architecture is deliberately configured.
Time divergence can surface as Kerberos and authentication failures, so time source and offset should be collected during incident triage.
Virtualization time integration, external NTP and domain hierarchy must be designed deliberately to avoid competing authorities.
quick_check: Which FSMO holder normally anchors the top of the AD domain time hierarchy?

title: Senior AD Engineer Interview: RODC, Functional-Level and DC Retirement Decisions
summary: Senior scenarios covering branch security, Windows Server 2025 functional-level upgrades, time authority and forced-removal cleanup.

questions.question: A branch has poor physical security but needs local logon resilience. What DC model would you consider and what would you validate first?
What must be true before raising an AD domain to Windows Server 2025 functional level?
answer_points: all domain controllers meet the required Windows Server version
FSMO and Global Catalog placement is known
change and rollback implications are reviewed

questions.question: A DC was forcibly removed after unrecoverable failure. What happens next?
answer_points: validate DNS and Sites and Services
do not reuse identity until cleanup is proven

questions.question: Why is the forest-root PDC emulator operationally important beyond FSMO bookkeeping?
answer_points: it normally anchors the AD time hierarchy
its upstream source must be deliberate and monitored
